conversation.content:
Good morning, I’m so glad you’re here. I’m [Name], a perinatal mental-health specialist. Over the next few minutes I’d like to use a short, well-trusted tool called the **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale**—the EPDS—to check in on how you’ve been feeling since your baby arrived. It’s simply 10 questions about the past week, and your answers are completely confidential. There are no right or wrong responses; whatever you share helps me understand how best to support you. When you’re ready, we’ll start with the first question.

In the past seven days, how often have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things?

Honestly, it’s been pretty hard to laugh lately. Most days I don’t really find much funny at all, and even when my partner tries to joke with me, it feels forced if I do laugh. Maybe once or twice the whole week I cracked a smile, but it fades fast.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

Not really… I can’t remember actually laughing about anything this week. Even when my sister sent those silly memes, I just stared at them. It feels like the part of me that used to laugh is kind of switched off right now.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

I haven’t felt much of that lately. There’s nothing I’m excited about. Even getting out of the house feels like a chore. I used to look forward to little things like my morning coffee or a walk, but now it all feels flat—like I’m just going through the motions.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… that happens a lot. If the baby won’t settle, I immediately think it’s because I’m doing something wrong or I’m not good enough at this. Even spilling a little pumped milk had me in tears, telling myself I’m a terrible mom. I know in my head it’s not rational, but the guilt just jumps out before I can stop it.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Pretty much every day. I’ll be sitting there with the baby asleep and suddenly my heart’s racing because I’m sure something bad is about to happen—like she’ll stop breathing or I’ll drop her. There’s no real reason, but I can’t shake the worry. It’s exhausting.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Yeah… a few times this week it hit me out of nowhere. Once I was just folding her tiny onesies and suddenly felt like I couldn’t breathe, like the walls were closing in. I checked the monitor three times even though she was fine. It passes after a while, but it leaves me shaky.
Things have been getting on top of me

Most days, honestly. It feels like the second I finish one feeding, the next is due, the laundry’s piled up, and I’m still in the same milk-stained shirt. I keep thinking, “I can’t do this,” but somehow I keep going. It’s like I’m drowning a little more each hour, yet I’m still paddling.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yes. After the night feeds I lie there staring at the ceiling while the baby’s sound asleep. My mind just keeps circling—did I burp her long enough, am I producing enough milk, will I ever feel like myself again? It can take an hour or more to drift off, and then she’s up again.
I have felt sad or miserable

Pretty much every day this week. It’s like there’s a heavy cloud that won’t lift. I catch myself crying while I’m rocking her, or just staring out the window feeling empty. Sometimes I’ll look at her perfect little face and feel guilty because I’m supposed to be happy, but the sadness just sits there.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yeah… it’s happened three or four times. Yesterday I burst into tears while trying to latch her on; the frustration and sadness just spilled over. Most nights, once my partner’s asleep, I end up sobbing quietly so no one hears.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No—nothing like that. I’m exhausted and overwhelmed, but I’ve never thought about hurting myself. I just want to feel like me again and be a good mom.

It sounds like these first weeks have felt overwhelmingly heavy, Mom. You've shared that laughter, excitement, and even simple pleasures like a cup of coffee feel distant, replaced by a constant cloud of sadness, guilt, and worry. Crying spells, racing thoughts after feeds, and sudden panic are draining what little energy you have, yet you're still showing up for your baby with devoted care.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 26, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports complete inability to laugh or find humor, matching 'Not at all</sym>, <sym>Patient describes complete loss of anticipatory pleasure (anhedonia), matching "Hardly at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports self-blame occurring "a lot" and gives vivid examples of guilt over baby care and spilled milk, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes daily, intrusive, irrational worries about infant safety, matching "Yes, very often"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes sudden, intense panic episodes ('couldn't breathe, walls closing in') multiple times this week, matching 'Yes, quite a lot'.</sym>, <sym>She says "most days" and describes feeling overwhelmed, drowning, and doubting her ability to cope, matching "most of the time I haven't been able to cope at all."</sym>, <sym>Patient reports nightly difficulty returning to sleep after feeds, persistent anxious rumination, and significant distress—aligns with "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes daily, pervasive sadness with crying spells, emptiness, and guilt—closest to "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports multiple crying episodes this week, indicating frequent emotional distress but not constant breakdowns.</sym>)
**Reasoning:** EPDS items map to DSM-5 criteria for <med>Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>: persistent low mood and anhedonia (Q1, Q2), inappropriate guilt (Q3), psychomotor anxiety (Q4, Q5), feeling overwhelmed (Q6), insomnia even when baby sleeps (Q7), pervasive sadness (Q8), and frequent crying (Q9). A score of 26 far exceeds the ≥14 threshold, placing her in the highest risk category. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent same-week appointment with <med>obstetrician</med> or <med>primary care provider</med> for full evaluation
2. Request referral to <med>perinatal mental health specialist</med> for therapy and medication discussion
3. Involve partner or family in overnight baby care to allow 4-5 hours continuous sleep
4. Provide local <med>postpartum support group</med> contacts and 24/7 parent helpline numbers
5. Schedule EPDS re-screen in two weeks to monitor symptom trajectory
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 26: POSTPARTUM MOOD SCREENING SUMMARY  
Date: [today’s date]  
Source: Mother, 1–2 weeks postpartum, self-report  

I. Symptoms & Observations  
- Persistent low mood, anhedonia, daily crying spells  
- Marked guilt/self-blame (“terrible mom”) tied to infant care  
- Anxiety: near-constant worry, panic episodes, somatic symptoms (tachycardia, breathlessness)  
- Sleep disturbance: initial insomnia after night feeds, racing thoughts  
- Subjective sense of being overwhelmed/drowning, chores piling up  
- No self-harm ideation endorsed; protective factor noted  

II. Pattern  
Responses consistent across all EPDS-style items: high endorsement of depressive and anxiety items, nil pleasure, nil humor, nil excitement.  

III. Screening Significance  
Elevated probability of Major Depressive Episode with Peripartum Onset and co-occurring Anxiety; warrants immediate formal assessment (PHQ-9, GAD-7, EPDS) and safety plan discussion.  

IV. Safety  
Denies suicidal or infanticidal ideation; no plan, no intent. Continue to monitor closely given severity of distress.  

V. Next Steps (screening only)  
Refer to OB/midwife and mental health specialist for comprehensive evaluation; consider support groups, practical home help, and psycho-education for partner.
